I've been trying to formalize Allen Hatcher's proof that CW complexes are Hausdorff. He begins by outlining a method (which I have implemented and called mkNhd) of generating open neighborhoods of some set AAA in a CW complex XXX by induction on skeleta, given a function (ε : (n : ℕ) → (j : 𝓔.Cells n) → ℝ that parameterizes the Hausdorff distance the preimage of the constructed neighborhood in each open cell is allowed to be from the preimage of AAA. Then, now working with two mkNhds on A,BA, BA,B simultaneously, he shows that given that at step n the two constructions are disjoint, there is a positive distance between the constructions and between each construction and the opposite base set A,BA, BA,B, and then concludes that it is possible to choose an ε so that the two constructions remain disjoint.

But that skips a step at the end: we need to know something about how mkNhd varies with respect to ε in order to say that "there exists some ε that makes the constructed neighborhoods small enough". We need a bound on, say, the Hausdorff distance between the constructed set and its base set, or we need that mkNhd is continuous, or something similar. But by inspection of Hatcher's method, the 'tight' bound on the Hausdorff distance turns out to be a complicated expression involving not just the dimension of the cell, but the value of ε at every cell its boundary intersects; loosening that bound to reference, say, iSup ε, breaks the induction because now you might have to reselect all previous choices of ε values in order to make the next step work out; and I have no idea how to begin to putting a topology on Set X so that I can even talk about continuous maps C((n : ℕ) → (j : 𝓔.Cells n) → ℝ, Set X).

Does anyone see either

  • a way to salvage this specific proof, or
  • a different, more convenient way of proving T2Space

I can work with? Or should I just leave this as a todo/proof wanted?

(I suppose I could just figure out how to work with said 'complicated expression', but even writing it down seems quite unpleasant and working with it is likely to be much worse, so I'm still in the market for alternative approaches.)

This is a very technical matter. Another approach using more general topology theory is due to Ernest Michael https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/colimits+of+paracompact+Hausdorff+spaces#ColimitsOfSequencesOfParacompacta

Apparently Topology.CWComplex in Mathlib can be non-Hausdorff: https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval/issues/657
Indeed one can see some declarations like Topology.RelCWComplex.isClosed_closedCell that assumes T2Space. Not sure about TopCat.CWComplex; there's nothing in Mathlib connecting both, maybe an AI can do it?
What is the point of mentioning AI for performing this task? This is complete nonsense.

TopCat.CWComplex indeed uses a categorical definition from which Hausdorff follows; I managed to prove that using some shenanigans with Gavrilovich-style separation-axioms-as-lifting-properties + using a colimit as a categorical recursor, which was much nicer. Sadly my PR apparently involves more infrastructure/helper definitions than the maintainers were willing to support, so it didn't go anywhere, as I recall.

So IIUC the two definitions are not equivalent (do not give the same class of spaces), contradicting this TODO in Mathlib. I mentioned AI because I thought if you write down the iff statement then AI (e.g. Aristotle) could quickly generate a certificate (proof), but now it seems that you need to add at least one condition.

They're equivalentish. The classical version indeed doesn't prove T2, but you can't actually use most of its API unless you have a T2 instance, and in the presence of a [T2Space] assumption they are interconvertible

About the equivalence between the two notions of CW-complexes, it seems to me that you have never shared a link towards a complete formalization of at least one of the directions. Publicizing this when creating PRs introducing new API (including some non superstandard notions) would be a significant incentive for reviewers as they would understand more easily that it is part of a path towards goals that we would like to have in mathlib.

I suppose. The problem is, I'm just not very good at Github, Github doesn't really do properly dependent PRs, and so the fact that every correction I make in an 'early' PR in a chain means I have to go remake all future PRs becomes a serious chore. That, and I did put up an entire direction in one go, which should have been a self-contained chunk in its own right; so the fact that that one got held up over what I thought of as minutiae and conveniences was rather demoralizing :wry:
